topic: Family Law: Muslim Law (Marriage, Dower, Talaq, and Inheritance)
description: This module explores the personal laws governing Muslims in India. It covers the contractual nature of Muslim marriage (Nikah), the essential concept of Dower (Mahr), various modes of dissolution of marriage (including the legal invalidity of Triple Talaq), and the foundational principles of Muslim inheritance and wills.

key_points: Nature of Nikah: Unlike a Hindu marriage which is a sacrament, a Muslim marriage (Nikah) is a civil contract. It requires a proposal (Ijab) from one party and acceptance (Qubool) from the other in the same meeting, usually in the presence of competent witnesses.

Mahr (Dower): It is a sum of money or other property which the wife is entitled to receive from the husband in consideration of the marriage. It is an absolute right of the wife and a mark of respect towards her.
Types of Mahr: It can be 'Prompt' (payable immediately on demand before or after the marriage) or 'Deferred' (payable on the dissolution of marriage by death or divorce).

dissolution_of_marriage_talaq.concept: Dissolution of Marriage and Triple Talaq
key_points: Modes of Divorce: A marriage can be dissolved by the husband (Talaq), by the wife (Khula - where she gives consideration to the husband for her release), or by mutual consent (Mubarat).
Talaq-e-Biddat (Triple Talaq): This was the practice of instantaneous and irrevocable divorce by pronouncing the word 'Talaq' three times in one sitting.

Legal Abolition: In the landmark Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) case, the Supreme Court declared Triple Talaq unconstitutional. Subsequently, the Parliament passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019, which makes the practice of instant Triple Talaq void, illegal, and a punishable criminal offense.

No Right by Birth: Muslim law does not recognize the concept of joint family property or a right to property by birth. Inheritance opens only on the death of the ancestor (Nemo est heres viventis - no one is the heir of a living person).
Rule of Shares: Generally, a male heir receives double the share of a female heir of the same degree (e.g., a son inherits twice as much as a daughter).

Restriction on Wills (Wasiyat): A Muslim cannot bequeath more than one-third (1/3rd) of their total property through a Will. The remaining two-thirds must devolve according to the strict rules of intestate succession among the legal heirs, unless the legal heirs consent to a larger bequest.

questions.question: Under Muslim law, what is the legal nature of 'Nikah' (marriage)?
questions.explanation: In Muslim law, Nikah is strictly defined as a civil contract between a man and a woman for the purpose of procreation and legalizing children. It requires offer, acceptance, and consideration (Mahr).

questions.question: A Muslim husband pronounces 'Talaq' three times in a fit of anger in a single sitting to his wife via a WhatsApp message in 2024. What is the legal validity of this divorce under current Indian law?

options.A: It is a valid and irrevocable divorce.
options.B: It is valid but revocable within 90 days.
options.C: It is completely void, illegal, and constitutes a criminal offense under the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.
options.D: It is valid only if approved by a local Sharia court.

questions.explanation: Following the Supreme Court's 2017 ruling and the subsequent 2019 Act, the practice of instantaneous 'Talaq-e-Biddat' (Triple Talaq), whether in spoken, written, or electronic form, is legally void and criminalized.

questions.question: A wealthy Muslim man, unhappy with his legal heirs, decides to write a Will (Wasiyat) leaving his entire estate (100% of his property) to a local charity. After his death, his legal heirs challenge the Will. What will be the legal outcome?

options.A: The Will is fully valid, and the charity gets 100% of the property.
options.B: The Will is completely void, and the charity gets nothing.
options.C: The Will is valid only up to one-third (1/3rd) of the property; the remaining two-thirds will go to the legal heirs.
options.D: The Will's validity will be decided by majority vote among the legal heirs.

questions.explanation: Under Muslim law, there is a strict restriction on testamentary power. A Muslim can only dispose of up to one-third (1/3rd) of their net estate by Will. The remaining two-thirds must go to the legal heirs according to the rules of inheritance, unless the heirs explicitly consent to the bequest exceeding one-third.
